headline: Harvest the last tender crops now — a killing frost can hit the Seacoast any night this week.

tasks.title: Pull tomatoes, peppers, squash, basil before a hard frost
tasks.detail: Mid-October is first-frost time on the Seacoast, and 28°F or below will finish tender crops overnight. Pick everything, including green tomatoes (ripen them indoors on a counter), and cut basil before it blackens.

tasks.title: Plant garlic
tasks.detail: Now through early November is the prime window. Split a head into cloves, plant pointy-end up 2-3 inches deep and 6 inches apart, then top with a few inches of straw or leaf mulch for next July's harvest.

tasks.title: Leave kale, carrots, and Brussels sprouts for the cold
tasks.detail: These hardy crops actually get sweeter after a light frost, so don't rush them. Keep picking as you need them — they'll hold in the ground for weeks yet.

tasks.title: Plant spring bulbs
tasks.detail: Get daffodils, tulips, and crocus in the ground before it freezes hard, roughly 2-3 times as deep as the bulb is tall, pointy-end up. They need these cool weeks to root for a spring show.

tasks.title: Clean up spent beds
tasks.detail: Pull finished plants and clear fallen leaves and fruit. Compost healthy material, but bag or trash anything with mildew, blight, or spots so disease doesn't overwinter in the soil.

tasks.title: Mulch beds and drain the hoses
tasks.detail: Spread a few inches of shredded leaves or straw over cleared beds to protect the soil, and disconnect and drain hoses before the first hard freeze so they don't split.
